Summary: Likelihood and bottom line
- Occupational asbestos exposure can contribute to COPD, and trades that involve sheet metal work—especially when combined with insulation, HVAC, pipefitting, and thermal-abatement tasks—have consistently shown elevated COPD risk compared with occupations without such exposures. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-0">Occupational pollutants such as mineral dusts and fibers are major contributors to COPD burden and synergize with smoking to greatly elevate risk</cite>. <cite id="01cf9c0c-0">Among older construction workers, 18% of COPD risk was attributable to job-related dusts, gases, and vapors acting independently or interactively, with broad exposure indices strongly predicting disease</cite>. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Construction trades with dust exposures (including insulators) show increased COPD risk, and specific cohorts of insulators demonstrate an association between asbestos exposure and COPD (approximately 44% increased risk) with dose–response evidence from Swedish gypsum/insulation particle exposure (about 56% increased risk)</cite>. 

- For a sheet metal worker exposed at low to moderate levels, the likelihood of developing COPD from asbestos alone is real but depends on cumulative dose and duration; risks rise with heavier and longer exposures and are lower for short, intermittent exposures. <cite id="3bcd06b8-0">Quantitative reviews conclude that heavy and prolonged chrysotile exposure can produce lung disease, and that low exposures may not yield detectable risk in aggregate analyses; risk depends on total dose over time</cite>. <cite id="3bcd06b8-4">Inhalation studies and epidemiologic syntheses support that biopersistent, respirable fibers drive persistent inflammation, proliferation, and fibrosis; amphibole asbestos is more biopersistent and potent than chrysotile, increasing disease likelihood for a given exposure</cite>.

What the evidence shows in construction trades and sheet-metal-related tasks
- Construction is a high‑risk sector for COPD, and within it, trades like insulation, roofing, sheet metal erection/repair, and related dust-generating tasks are implicated. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">In a large Ontario worker cohort, construction workers had increased COPD risk; excess risk clustered in trades including insulation, roofing, and structural metal erection/repair, with insulators specifically associated with COPD and prior analyses reporting about 44% increased risk linked to asbestos exposure</cite>. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Swedish evidence showed a positive exposure–response for particles from gypsum and insulation materials (about 56% increased risk)</cite>. <cite id="01cf9c0c-1">A U.S. study reported a 34% increased COPD risk overall among construction workers, with even higher risks in specific trades (e.g., roofers and cement masons/bricklayers), consistent with dust-driven mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="01cf9c0c-4">Systematic reviews focused on construction trades and included insulation workers, ironworkers, roofers, and related roles, confirming higher COPD risk with occupational dust exposures</cite>. 

- Sheet metal work overlaps with these hazards: installing/removing fibrous insulation, working with sprayed-on thermal shields, and abatement can involve inhalation of chrysotile (white) asbestos and other mineral fibers, metal dusts, and cement/silica aerosols. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Excess COPD among insulators plausibly reflects application, removal, and repair of insulating materials (including asbestos-containing products), and asbestos exposure in Canadian insulators was associated with COPD</cite>. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-4">In a construction case-control study, asbestos was among the agents significantly associated with COPD risk alongside welding, silica, and cement dusts</cite>. Although some systematic reviews list “sheet metal work” as an exclusion, the airborne fiber/dust milieu is shared, and COPD risks there are elevated when exposures are substantial and sustained. <cite id="01cf9c0c-3">Exclusion lists for COPD studies in construction sometimes include sheet metal work, likely because exposure patterns are complex and often combined with asbestos and silica; nonetheless, COPD risk is elevated across these trades when exposures are present</cite>.

Mechanisms, fiber properties, and dose–response
- Asbestos pathogenicity depends on three principles: biologic activity (dose), fiber dimension (length and critical length ~5 µm), and durability/biopersistence. <cite id="3bcd06b8-4">Recent inhalation studies and epidemiologic analyses show that respirable, biopersistent fibers cause persistent pulmonary inflammation, cell proliferation, fibrosis, and cancer; amphibole fibers are more biopersistent and potent than chrysotile, which is less biopersistent but still capable of producing pathology at high or cumulative doses</cite>. <cite id="3bcd06b8-2">An exposure concentration of 10 mg/m3 corresponds to more than 10 million times the ACGIH TLV of 0.1 fibers/cm3 by number; at such high gravimetric doses, macrophage clearance is impaired and non-specific inflammatory and proliferative responses (fibrosis and cancer) can occur</cite>. 

- Across fiber types, long, thin, biopersistent fibers drive disease risk; short fibers (<5 µm) contribute little to tumor risk, and mineralogy matters. <cite id="3bcd06b8-4">Structures <5 µm in length do not appear to contribute to lung tumor risk; mineralogy and crystal structure influence mesothelioma risk, with amphiboles more potent than chrysotile for mesothelioma</cite>. <cite id="3bcd06b8-0">Chrysotile is rapidly degraded in macrophage-rich lung environments, disintegrating into short fibers and particles, whereas amphibole persists and elicits interstitial fibrosis and pleural inflammation; amphiboles are more likely to cause asbestosis-like changes</cite>. 

- Cumulative exposure over time increases COPD likelihood; intermittent “low” exposures may yield modest absolute risks, while moderate-to-heavy, chronic exposures meaningfully elevate risk. <cite id="3bcd06b8-0">Heavy and prolonged exposure to chrysotile can produce lung cancer, and low exposures may not show detectable risk in aggregate analyses; total dose over time governs disease likelihood and progression</cite>. <cite id="3bcd06b8-2">Dose–response is highly sensitive to exposure concentration and duration, with overload conditions at high levels producing pronounced inflammation and fibrogenic responses</cite>.

How much risk in sheet metal workers?
- For sheet metal workers with low-to-moderate, intermittent exposure (e.g., years of dust-laden tasks without heavy airborne fiber burden), COPD risk is increased relative to unexposed workers but likely smaller than in trades with continuous exposure to friable asbestos products or high-concentration dust environments. <cite id="01cf9c0c-0">Across construction trades, combined VGDF exposures confer strong COPD risk, and occupational exposures can account for a substantial fraction of COPD cases</cite>. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Insulators exposed to asbestos-containing materials show about 44% increased COPD risk; Swedish data show ~56% increased risk with higher particle exposure from gypsum/insulation materials</cite>. 

- Fiber type and co-contaminants matter. If the sheet metal environment includes amphibole-containing products or mixed cement/silica dusts, risk is higher for a given exposure level. <cite id="8fdafa20-0">Amphibole fibers are generally more potent than chrysotile for asbestos-related diseases; many occupational exposures (e.g., shipyard, insulators) were to amphiboles</cite>. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Excess COPD risk among insulators plausibly reflects insulating materials, gypsum, and asbestos; asbestos exposure per se is associated with COPD</cite>. 

- Smoking multiplies risk and blunts protective clearance mechanisms, making “moderate” occupational exposure substantially more damaging. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-0">Synergism between occupational exposures and tobacco smoke greatly elevates COPD risk beyond additive individual effects</cite>. <cite id="8fdafa20-4">In a Chinese asbestos factory cohort, age- and smoking-adjusted hazard ratios for respiratory disease and lung cancer were elevated (e.g., respiratory disease HR 3.23), and in a nested case–control, smoking substantially increased lung cancer odds (OR 3.33), with high-exposure smokers having OR ~10 vs low-exposure non-smokers</cite>. Although smoking data for COPD are from lung cancer cohorts, the same mechanism of impaired clearance and oxidative stress applies, and joint exposure to dust plus smoking is a known driver of COPD in construction cohorts. <cite id="01cf9c0c-0">Construction-related exposures are additive to smoking in driving COPD risk</cite>.

Latency and clinical phenotype
- Asbestos-related lung disease typically has long latency (decades), consistent with chronic inflammatory and fibrotic processes. <cite id="3bcd06b8-4">Well-designed inhalation toxicity studies show that the dose–dimension–durability paradigm underpins asbestos pathologies; persistent fibers drive chronic inflammation and fibrosis over time</cite>. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Excess COPD risk has been observed among trades with cumulative dust exposure over long durations (e.g., insulation and related), implicating long-term occupational exposures</cite>. Clinically, asbestos exposure more strongly associates with asbestosis (restrictive physiology, pleural/parenchymal changes), whereas COPD with prominent chronic bronchitis and emphysema can coexist with asbestos exposure in mixed-dust settings; in cohort/occupational studies, asbestos is among multiple agents driving COPD phenotypes. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-4">Asbestos exposure was significantly associated with COPD risk in construction workers, alongside welding, silica, and cement dusts</cite>. 

Practical risk assessment for a sheet metal worker
- If you were a sheet metal worker with years of exposure to dusts and occasional asbestos-containing materials, your lifetime risk of COPD would be elevated compared with unexposed individuals, with risk scaling with cumulative exposure (task intensity, duration, and fiber concentration) and co-exposures (silica, cement, welding fumes) and smoking status. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Insulators and structural metal trades show elevated COPD risk, with asbestos per se associated with ~44% higher risk and positive exposure–response to gypsum/insulation particles</cite>. <cite id="3bcd06b8-0">Total dose over time governs likelihood; low aggregate exposures may not show detectable risk in aggregate analyses, but do increase risk compared with minimal exposure</cite>. To personalize risk, consider:
  - Exposure intensity: frequent cutting/grinding/abatement of fibrous insulation or asbestos-containing sheet goods increases airborne fiber load.
  - Duration: 10+ years of intermittent exposure raises cumulative dose beyond short episodes.
  - Fiber mix: presence of amphibole or high crystallinity/elongation increases biopersistence and disease potency.
  - Smoking: even light-to-moderate smoking multiplies COPD risk and accelerates lung function decline.
  Screening spirometry and careful exposure history can help identify early airflow limitation or small-airway disease; if asbestos fibers are suspected, chest HRCT and environmental sampling can guide risk triage. <cite id="01cf9c0c-0">Construction workers with heavy VGDF exposure are at elevated COPD risk and benefit from control measures and smoking cessation</cite>. 

Uncertainty and what clarifies it
- Quantifying COPD risk per unit of chrysotile fiber (fibers/mL-year) is less developed than for lung cancer, and studies vary in exposure metrics (PCOM vs gravimetric vs mineralogical analysis), making cross-study comparisons challenging. <cite id="3bcd06b8-2">Dose–response varies with fiber length distribution, non-fibrous particle load, and exposure overload; an asbestos concentration of 10 mg/m3 is orders of magnitude above TLVs, complicating translation to lower levels</cite>. More granular exposure assessment (MMF/microscopy with quantitative fiber metrics and mineralogy) and trade-specific cohort studies would sharpen risk estimates. <cite id="8fdafa20-0">Reviews emphasize fiber type and exposure reconstruction; amphibole vs chrysotile potency and co-occurrence complicate risk estimation</cite>. Clinically, COPD attributable to asbestos may present with features overlapping other dust exposures; careful job history and serial lung function testing remain essential. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-4">Construction-related COPD phenotypes reflect mixed exposures; asbestos is a confirmed contributor</cite>.

Actionable takeaways
- The likelihood that low-to-moderate asbestos exposure (e.g., as a sheet metal worker handling insulation or performing abatement) can cause COPD is nontrivial: COPD risk in exposed trades is consistently elevated and scales with cumulative exposure, fiber biopersistence, and co-exposures, with synergism from smoking. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Insulators show ~44% COPD increase with asbestos exposure and dose–response to gypsum/insulation particles</cite>. <cite id="01cf9c0c-0">Across construction workers, occupational exposures explain 18% of COPD risk and are additive to smoking</cite>. 
- For “low to moderate” exposures, expect a moderate relative increase compared with minimal-exposure peers, especially if exposure was long enough and co-exposures (e.g., silica/cement, welding) were present; short and infrequent exposures pose lower risk. <cite id="3bcd06b8-0">Risk rises with heavy and prolonged exposure; low exposures may not show detectable aggregate risk but still increase absolute risk</cite>. 
- Minimize risk: engineering controls (local exhaust, HEPA vacuums), work practices (wet methods), respirators, elimination of amphibole-containing materials when possible, and smoking cessation. <cite id="01cf9c0c-0">Preventing exposure and promoting smoking cessation are key interventions in construction workers</cite>. 

Practical summary
- If you were a sheet metal worker with years of dust exposure (including potential asbestos) and do not smoke heavily, your lifetime COPD risk is elevated but lower than in trades with continuous heavy asbestos exposure; if you smoked, risk is substantially higher. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Insulators with asbestos exposure had ~44% increased COPD risk, with dose–response to insulation/gypsum particles</cite>. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-0">Occupational exposures account for roughly 10–21% of COPD globally and synergize with smoking</cite>. <cite id="3bcd06b8-4">Long, thin, biopersistent fibers drive chronic lung injury; amphiboles are more potent than chrysotile, and risk accumulates over time</cite>. A spirometric evaluation and detailed exposure history are advisable, particularly if you have 10+ years of exposure, frequent dust-generating tasks, or co-exposures, and if you smoked. <cite id="01cf9c0c-0">Construction-related exposures are independently predictive of COPD and are additive to smoking risk</cite>.

Title: Health risk of chrysotile revisited
Snippet: Abstract This review provides a basis for substantiating both kinetically and pathologically the differences between chrysotile and amphibole asbestos. Chrysotile, which is rapidly attacked by the acid environment of the macrophage, falls apart in the lung into short fibers and particles, while the amphibole asbestos persist creating a response to the fibrous structure of this mineral. Inhalation toxicity studies of chrysotile at non-lung overload conditions demonstrate that the long (>20 µm) fibers are rapidly cleared from the lung, are not translocated to the pleural cavity and do not initiate fibrogenic response. In contrast, long amphibole asbestos fibers persist, are quickly (within 7 d) translocated to the pleural cavity and result in interstitial fibrosis and pleural inflammation. Quantitative reviews of epidemiological studies of mineral fibers have determined the potency of chrysotile and amphibole asbestos for causing lung cancer and mesothelioma in relation to fiber type and have also differentiated between these two minerals. These studies have been reviewed in light of the frequent use of amphibole asbestos. As with other respirable particulates, there is evidence that heavy and prolonged exposure to chrysotile can produce lung cancer. The importance of the present and other similar reviews is that the studies they report show that low exposures to chrysotile do not present a detectable risk to health. Since total dose over time decides the likelihood of disease occurrence and progression, they also suggest that the risk of an adverse outcome may be low with even high exposures experienced over a short duration.
</snippet>

Fiber types sometimes occur in combination, e.g., chrysotile from Quebec, Canada, typically contains approxi- mately 1% of tremolite, an amphibole. - Asbestos-related lung disease typically has long latency (decades), consistent with chronic inflammatory and fibrotic processes. <cite id="3bcd06b8-4">Well-designed inhalation toxicity studies show that the dose–dimension–durability paradigm underpins asbestos pathologies; persistent fibers drive chronic inflammation and fibrosis over time</cite>. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Excess COPD risk has been observed among trades with cumulative dust exposure over long durations (e.g., insulation and related), implicating long-term occupational exposures</cite>. - If you were a sheet metal worker with years of exposure to dusts and occasional asbestos-containing materials, your lifetime risk of COPD would be elevated compared with unexposed individuals, with risk scaling with cumulative exposure (task intensity, duration, and fiber concentration) and co-exposures (silica, cement, welding fumes) and smoking status. <cite id="b8ebf4c2-2">Insulators and structural metal trades show elevated COPD risk, with asbestos per se associated with ~44% higher risk and positive exposure–response to gypsum/insulation particles</cite>. <cite id="3bcd06b8-0">Total dose over time governs likelihood; low aggregate exposures may not show detectable risk in aggregate analyses, but do increase risk compared with minimal exposure</cite>.   - Smoking: even light-to-moderate smoking multiplies COPD risk and accelerates lung function decline.

- Quantifying COPD risk per unit of chrysotile fiber (fibers/mL-year) is less developed than for lung cancer, and studies vary in exposure metrics (PCOM vs gravimetric vs mineralogical analysis), making cross-study comparisons challenging. <cite id="3bcd06b8-2">Dose–response varies with fiber length distribution, non-fibrous particle load, and exposure overload; an asbestos concentration of 10 mg/m3 is orders of magnitude above TLVs, complicating translation to lower levels</cite>. Title: Beyond Smoking: Emerging Drivers of COPD and Their Clinical Implications in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Narrative Review
Snippet: Occupational exposure significantly contributes to the COPD burden, particularly in LMICs, yet remains frequently underrecognized. Industries such as mining, construction, agriculture, metal and foundry work, textile production, automotive repair, and informal jobs involving biomass smoke notably affect lung health, especially among women in rural areas [43][44][45][46]. 

Occupational pollutants exacerbate COPD symptoms, causing increased airflow limitation, frequent exacerbations, and higher rates of hospitalization [44,[47][48][49]. Common symptoms include chronic sputum production, dyspnea, and reduced quality of life. Notably, the combined exposure to tobacco smoke and occupational pollutants synergistically elevates COPD risk beyond individual effects [43]. 

Occupational exposure accounts for approximately 10-21% of COPD cases globally, with higher prevalence in specific occupations and regions [43,45,[50][51][52]. Harmful exposures include mineral and biological dust, diesel exhaust, welding fumes, pesticides, and organic particles. Agricultural and textile workers exposed to biological dust show relative risks (RRs) between 1.33 and 1.6; miners and construction workers exposed to silica and mineral dust have hazard ratios (HRs) ranging from 1.46 to 1.71; welding fumes and diesel exhaust present additional HRs of 1.57 and 1.18, respectively. Agricultural pesticide exposure carries a particularly high risk (RR 2.2), and biomass smoke exposure among women in LMICs has an odds ratio (OR) above 1.5 [43][44][45][46]51]. The FLOW study, which examined 1202 patients with COPD, reported an increased COPD risk associated with exposure to vapors, gas, dust, or fumes (VGDF) (OR 2.11; 95% CI 1.59-2.82; PAF 31%). Using a job exposure matrix (JEM), they found an OR of 2.27 (95% CI 1.46-3.52; PAF 13%) [43]. 

The co-occurrence of occupational exposures and smoking substantially heightens COPD risk.

Title: Exposure to occupational risk factors is associated with the severity and progression of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Snippet: According to American Thoracic Association, occupational risk factor exposure accounts for 10 to 20% of the COPD cases. [9] n this study, among 4082 COPD investigated patients, 1063 cases were found to have a history of exposure to different kinds of occupational risk factors during their occupational career (accounted for 26.0%) which is higher than that American Thoracic Association reported. Females in the exposure group accounted for 41.5%, but 30.2% in the non-exposure group, suggesting that occupational risk factor exposure may have a greater impact on females than males. 

In a study of 94,551 never-smokers in the population-based UK Biobank cohort, Matteis [10] found that manufacturing is the sector with the highest risk of COPD, and agriculture also has a significantly increased risk of COPD. Hnizdo [11] conducted a study on 9823 US population-based Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey and the results showed that ORs for COPD were increased for the following industries: rubber, plastics, and leather manufacturing; utilities; office building services; textile mill products manufacturing; the armed forces; food products manufacturing; repair services and gas stations; agriculture; sales; construction; transportation and trucking; personal services; and health care. Our study found that the occupational risk factor exposure rates among the COPD patients in different industries were different. The top 3 industries with a large number of COPD cases and a history of exposure to occupational risk factors were agriculture (including farming, forestry, animal husbandry, and fishery), manufacturing, and mining. There are many occupational hazards in these types of work environments. For example, people engaged in agriculture can be exposed to grain dust; those engaged in animal husbandry can be exposed to animal dust; those engaged in coal mining can be exposed to coal dust, silica dust, or metallic dust; and those engaged in chemical manufacturing can be exposed to irritating gases and fumes. Workers engaged in these industries and occupations normally were not very well educated resulting in insufficient knowledge of occupational risk factor exposure and low awareness of personal protection. Therefore, special attention should be paid to the prevalence, prevention, and control of COPD in these industries and occupations.

Title: Risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a large cohort of Ontario, Canada workers
Snippet: Increased risk of COPD was observed among workers in construction, transportation, farming, forestry, mining, and processing. Patterns for these jobs, where common exposures include organic and inorganic dust and diesel exhaust, were similarly increased for males and females. Notable sex differences in risk of COPD were also identified in this study, particularly among service occupations. This study attempted to indirectly adjust for smoking by applying prevalence estimates that were generated using provincial population survey data. Findings showed that there were no significant differences in risk when adjusting for cigarette smoking. Although this is not based on the true smoking status of workers in the ODSS cohort, this study sought out a method to include population smoking data to address cigarette smoking. This study found that the risk among construction workers (predominately male) was driven by those employed in excavating, grading and related; concrete finishing and related; painting, paperhanging and related; insulation; roofing, waterproofing and related; structural metal erecting; glazier work; labour and elemental work; and other construction trades (e.g., brick and stone masons, carpenters, plasters). Similar to this study, a recent US study reported a 34% increased risk of COPD among construction workers compared to non-construction workers 12 . They reported the highest risks among roofers (122% increased risk) and cement masons/bricklayers (136% increased risk) 12 . Another study in the UK observed higher risks of COPD among roofers, floorers and www.nature.com/scientificreports/ labourers, but not for masons or bricklayers 18 . It is likely that these workers are exposed to respirable dust given the nature of their work. The excess risk observed among insulators in this study may be due to exposures during the application, removal and repair of thermal shields in buildings and pipes, including insulating materials, gypsum, and asbestos. A recent study of Canadian insulators reported an association (44% increased risk) between asbestos exposure and COPD 19 . A Swedish study reported finding a positive exposure-response relationship among males exposed to particles from gypsum and insulation material (56% increased risk) 20 .

Title: Risk of lung cancer according to mild steel and stainless steel welding.
Snippet: The participants were selected from a cohort of 10 059 male production workers employed at Danish companies handling stainless steel or mild steel for a minimum of 1 year within the period April 1964 through December 1984. The cohort members were male metal workers, alive as of April 1968 and born before 1 January 1965. 

To minimize the incompleteness of the registration of the cohort members, the cohort was created in two phases with the use of two independent data sources (1,23). In phase one, the companies included in the study were asked to establish a roster of men who had ever been employed as production workers. In phase two, additional company workers were identified from records of the Danish Pension Fund and the Danish Central Population Registry. All wage earners in Denmark have been compulsory members of this pension scheme since 1964, and records have been kept even when a person has retired, emigrated, or deceased. Title: Health risk of chrysotile revisited
Snippet: Abstract This review provides a basis for substantiating both kinetically and pathologically the differences between chrysotile and amphibole asbestos. Chrysotile, which is rapidly attacked by the acid environment of the macrophage, falls apart in the lung into short fibers and particles, while the amphibole asbestos persist creating a response to the fibrous structure of this mineral. Inhalation toxicity studies of chrysotile at non-lung overload conditions demonstrate that the long (>20 µm) fibers are rapidly cleared from the lung, are not translocated to the pleural cavity and do not initiate fibrogenic response. In contrast, long amphibole asbestos fibers persist, are quickly (within 7 d) translocated to the pleural cavity and result in interstitial fibrosis and pleural inflammation. Quantitative reviews of epidemiological studies of mineral fibers have determined the potency of chrysotile and amphibole asbestos for causing lung cancer and mesothelioma in relation to fiber type and have also differentiated between these two minerals. These studies have been reviewed in light of the frequent use of amphibole asbestos. As with other respirable particulates, there is evidence that heavy and prolonged exposure to chrysotile can produce lung cancer. The importance of the present and other similar reviews is that the studies they report show that low exposures to chrysotile do not present a detectable risk to health. Since total dose over time decides the likelihood of disease occurrence and progression, they also suggest that the risk of an adverse outcome may be low with even high exposures experienced over a short duration.

The cohort and case-control studies evaluated both pleural and peritoneal mesotheliomas, with some studies not discerning between the two sites. When reported, the workers via whom the individuals were domestically exposed were nearly always exposed to amphiboles. This fiber-type issue is further complicated by the fact that some chrysotile deposits have different degrees of co-occurrence of tremolite.

Therefore, special attention should be paid to the prevalence, prevention, and control of COPD in these industries and occupations.

The current study endeavors to elucidate the effects of dust exposure and smoking on COPD incidence amongst coal mine workers, while concurrently devising preventive strategies for this affliction. Method A nested case–control study was conducted encompassing 1,416 participants aged ≥ 18 years, spanning the duration from (2017–2018) until 2020. Multiple logistic regression analysis was employed to scrutinize the associations between smoking, dust exposure with COPD among coal workers. Following meticulous adjustment for confounding variables, it was discerned that cumulative dust exposure within the range of 47.19 ~ (OR: 1.90, 95% CI: 1.05, 3.44), 101.27 ~ (OR: 1.99, 95% CI: 1.17, 3.39), as well as smoking indices of 72 ~ (OR: 1.85, 95% CI: 1.19, 2.88), 145 ~ (OR: 1.74, 95% CI: 1.17, 2.61), 310 ~ (OR: 1.85, 95% CI: 1.23, 2.77) engender an escalated vulnerability to COPD among coal workers. Conclusion Dust exposure and smoking were unequivocally identified as precipitating risk factors for COPD incidence within the population of coal workers, albeit devoid of any discernible interaction between these two causal agents.

We included cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies published in peer-reviewed papers if (i) the exposure included construction trades, job titles in the construction industry or dust among construction workers; (ii) the outcome was a spirometry-based definition of airway obstruction, physician-diagnosed COPD, chronic bronchitis or pulmonary emphysema (including cause of death registered on death certificates) or selfreported symptoms of chronic bronchitis (cough and sputum production for at least 3 months per year for at least 2 years) and (iii) there was an analysis of risk by occupation or occupational exposure. Exclusion criteria for the studies were (i) the exposure was defined as brick manufacturing, boilermaking, heavy clay industry, cement factory work, tunnel work, asphalt work, sheet metal work, mining, asbestos, silica, non-specific vapour/ gas/dust/fumes or where construction workers were combined with other workers without separate analyses on the construction workers; (ii) the outcome was asthma or pneumoconiosis or (iii) the study did not include a reference group or internal comparator. 

For each of the included papers, we used a data extraction sheet used in a recent review on COPD [5] comprising details of the study design, selection of the study sample, characteristics of the study population and comparison group, response rate, sample size, degree and duration of exposure, the outcome studied and confounders considered. We did not reanalyse any of the data in the papers. An evaluation of the quality of the studies was performed independently by two of the authors (C.B. and L.K.). Disagreements were resolved by discussion between the two. Table 1 shows the items in the quality assessment. The items could be scored as positive or negative, where a positive score denoted less risk of bias. We did not sum up the positive ratings to a quality score, because the items were not of equal importance (Table 2).

For example, 577 asbestos workers and 435 control workers were followed from 1972 to 2008, and 259 deaths were identified in the asbestos cohort [7]. Of these 259 individuals, the major cause-specific fatalities included 96 deaths from various cancers, such as lung cancer (n = 53) and non-malignant respiratory diseases (n = 81). In contrast, the control cohort included nine cases of lung cancer and 11 cases of respiratory diseases. The age-and smoking-adjusted hazard ratios for mortality by all causes and all cancers in asbestos workers were 2.05 (95% CI 1.56-2.68) and 1.89 (95% CI 1.25-2.87), respectively, whereas those for lung cancer and respiratory diseases were 3.31 (95% CI 1.60-6.87) and 3.23 (95% CI 1.68-6.22), respectively. 

A nested case-control study was conducted with workers from the same factory [8]. Of the 1139 asbestos workers who had ever worked there for longer than 1 year, there were 41 male individuals with lung cancer in 2001 and each case was matched according to age (± 5 years) with five control subjects. A conditional logistic regression model was performed to estimate the odds ratios (ORs) of lung cancer risk associated with different exposure levels and revealed that 54% of cases had high exposure and 24% had low exposure while 24% of controls had high exposure and 44% had low exposure; smoking was more common in the cancer cohort (90%) than in the control group (73%). The adjusted OR for lung cancer was 3.66 (95% CI 1.61-8.29) for the high-exposure group and was slightly elevated for the medium-exposure group (OR 1.25; 95% CI 0.47-3.31); additionally, smoking was related to lung cancer risk (OR 3.33; 95% CI 1.10-10.08). Compared to the  low-exposure non-smoking group, the ORs were 10.39 (95% CI 1.34-82.45) for the high-exposure smoking group and 5.23 (95% CI 0.50-54.58)

Summary answer
As a sheet metal worker, low-to-moderate, long-duration exposure to asbestos materially increases the likelihood of COPD, and this risk persists independently of smoking, though the magnitude depends on exposure dose and timing. Based on occupational cohort and cross-sectional evidence, excess COPD mortality and obstructive spirometric impairment are seen at cumulative exposures well below the highest industrial levels, and analyses adjusted for smoking—including in nonsmokers—still show adverse effects of asbestos exposure on airflow and diffusion capacity. Smoking potentiates these effects via impaired fiber clearance and synergistic interactions documented for related asbestos-related lung disease; thus, in practice, sheet metal exposure should be considered an independent COPD risk alongside smoking, with the combined effect notably higher than either alone. <cite id="9c43250d-2">Asbestos exposure contributes to obstructive airway impairment, with about 2.5× higher obstructive dysfunction than controls, and even when comparing nonsmoking asbestos workers to nonsmoker controls, exposed workers show lower FEV1/FVC and reduced predicted FEV1/FVC, DLCO, and FEV1</cite> <cite id="8c695b82-3">After adjusting for age and smoking, asbestos exposure remained associated with restrictive patterns and reduced DLCO, and in nonsmokers only, asbestos exposure was significantly associated with lower predicted FEV1, FVC, and DLCO</cite> <cite id="cf6a0c42-0">In Libby asbestos-exposed workers, COPD mortality (SMR 2.2, 95% CI 1.7–2.9) was elevated even after a 15-year lag and among those with cumulative exposure < 4.5 fibers/cm³-years, with nonmalignant respiratory disease excess also present at low cumulative exposures</cite> <cite id="8c695b82-1">Reviews note asbestos can cause pulmonary obstruction distinct from smoking; smoking and asbestos act synergistically, with higher profusion of pleural disease in smokers associated with more obstructive spirometry</cite> <cite id="9c43250d-4">Mechanistic plausibility includes impaired mucociliary clearance and increased airway permeability with smoking facilitating deeper penetration of asbestos fibers</cite>.

- Cohort and population cohort evidence: Occupational cohorts exposed to asbestos show elevated COPD mortality and broader nonmalignant respiratory disease even at modest cumulative exposure levels. In the Libby vermiculite cohort, allowing a 15-year lag produced an SMR of 2.2 for COPD overall, and excess nonmalignant respiratory disease mortality was seen at cumulative exposures below 4.5 fibers/cm³-years; nonmalignant respiratory disease rose to 4.8-fold at ≥300 fibers/cm³-years. Title: Additive Synergism between Asbestos and Smoking in Lung Cancer Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Snippet: Smoking and asbestos exposure are important risks for lung cancer. Several epidemiological studies have linked asbestos exposure and smoking to lung cancer. To reconcile and unify these results, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to provide a quantitative estimate of the increased risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure and cigarette smoking and to classify their interaction. Five electronic databases were searched from inception to May, 2015 for observational studies on lung cancer. All case-control (N = 10) and cohort (N = 7) studies were included in the analysis. Lung cancer patients who were not exposed to asbestos and non-smoking (A-S-) were compared with; (i) asbestos-exposed and non-smoking (A+S-), (ii) non-exposure to asbestos and smoking (A-S+), and (iii) asbestos-exposed and smoking (A+S+). Our meta-analysis showed a significant difference in risk of developing lung cancer among asbestos exposed and/or smoking workers compared to controls (A-S-), odds ratios for the disease (95% CI) were (i) 1.70 (A+S-, 1.31–2.21), (ii) 5.65; (A-S+, 3.38–9.42), (iii) 8.70 (A+S+, 5.8–13.10). The additive interaction index of synergy was 1.44 (95% CI = 1.26–1.77) and the multiplicative index = 0.91 (95% CI = 0.63–1.30). Corresponding values for cohort studies were 1.11 (95% CI = 1.00–1.28) and 0.51 (95% CI = 0.31–0.85). Assessments of industrial health risks should take smoking and other airborne health risks when setting occupational asbestos exposure limits.

Two hundred seventy seven asbestos workers and 177 control subjects were included in the study ( Table 1). The participation rates for exposed and control subjects were not different: 77% and 80% respectively. The asbestos workers were significantly older than the controls. Smoking was more frequent among asbestos workers, and they also had smoked a greater number of pack years. Among the asbestos workers, 36% had radiographic changes consistent with emphysema, 31% with asbestosis, and 15% had CXR findings consistent with both asbestosis and emphysema.

As shown in figure 1, more than 80% of the controls had normal pulmonary function compared to only half of the asbestos workers had normal pulmonary function. Consequently, the proportions of subjects with obstructive, restrictive and mixed patterns of pulmonary dys- function in the exposed group were all higher than the corresponding proportions in the control group.

Although the PFT values except the FEV1/FVC ratio were adjusted for age and height, we also included age in the regression analysis as there was significant age difference between the exposed and control groups ( Table 2). Because we were interested in examining the effect of mere asbestos exposure (without CXR evidence of asbestosis) on patterns of pulmonary, we excluded patients with radiographic asbestosis from the model. After accounting for age and smoking, asbestos exposure was significantly associated with restrictive pattern of pulmonary dysfunction and decreased DLCO. However, asbestos exposure was not significantly associated with FEV1/ FVC ratio. Similar results were found when FEV1, FVC, and DLCO were regressed on exposure status and pack year without including age in the model (not shown).

As shown in Table 3, when PFT values were regressed on exposure status in non-smokers only, asbestos exposure was significantly associated with low FEV1, FVC and DLCO percent predicted values after accounting for age. documents.title: Additive Synergism between Asbestos and Smoking in Lung Cancer Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
documents.snippet: Smoking and asbestos exposure are important risks for lung cancer. Several epidemiological studies have linked asbestos exposure and smoking to lung cancer. To reconcile and unify these results, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to provide a quantitative estimate of the increased risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure and cigarette smoking and to classify their interaction. Five electronic databases were searched from inception to May, 2015 for observational studies on lung cancer. All case-control (N = 10) and cohort (N = 7) studies were included in the analysis. We calculated pooled odds ratios (ORs), relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using a random-effects model for the association of asbestos exposure and smoking with lung cancer. Lung cancer patients who were not exposed to asbestos and non-smoking (A-S-) were compared with; (i) asbestos-exposed and non-smoking (A+S-), (ii) non-exposure to asbestos and smoking (A-S+), and (iii) asbestos-exposed and smoking (A+S+). Our meta-analysis showed a significant difference in risk of developing lung cancer among asbestos exposed and/or smoking workers compared to controls (A-S-), odds ratios for the disease (95% CI) were (i) 1.70 (A+S-, 1.31–2.21), (ii) 5.65; (A-S+, 3.38–9.42), (iii) 8.70 (A+S+, 5.8–13.10). The additive interaction index of synergy was 1.44 (95% CI = 1.26–1.77) and the multiplicative index = 0.91 (95% CI = 0.63–1.30). Corresponding values for cohort studies were 1.11 (95% CI = 1.00–1.28) and 0.51 (95% CI = 0.31–0.85). Our results point to an additive synergism for lung cancer with co-exposure of asbestos and cigarette smoking. Assessments of industrial health risks should take smoking and other airborne health risks when setting occupational asbestos exposure limits.

Title: Prevalence of risk for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease amongst carpenters using lung function questionnaire
Snippet: Background: An obstructive ventilatory pattern is a hallmark of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a slow-progressing respiratory condition that is frequently linked to cigarette use and can result in chronic respiratory failure. A case-finding tool called the lung function questionnaire (LFQ) is being created to help doctors choose which patients should undergo spirometry testing to confirm the presence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Methods: Survey research study of 185 convenient sampling.
Results: The results were obtained using lung function questionnaire. Statistical analysis shows that there is prevalence of risk for COPD amongst the carpenters.
Conclusions: This study concludes that there is a risk of developing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in carpenters who are exposed to saw dust as more than half the samples have scored less than or equal to 18 which indicates the risk for COPD.

Title: Occupation and 11-year lung function decline in the HUNT Study
Snippet: Occupational exposure to vapours, dust, gas and fumes (VGDF) can cause or exacerbate respiratory symptoms and lung disease [1,2]. It has been estimated that ~15% of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) cases are attributable to preventable occupational exposures [3]. 

Identifying high-risk occupations is important for implementing targeted interventions. Many studies have investigated exposure to VGDF, as summarized in reviews [4][5][6]. Further, a review outlined studies of VGDF identified by a jobexposure matrix [7]. Although occupational titles give a coarse exposure classification, as the harmful agent is not specified and exposure can vary within the same occupation, it provides important knowledge to target risk reduction measures. Few studies have examined lung function across a variety of jobs titles [8][9][10][11][12][13], an approach that increases the chance to detect all high-risk jobs. To our knowledge, only one study has provided longitudinal spirometry measurements [13], which enables the examination of intraindividual changes and enhances precision and validity. The study indicated a higher incidence of COPD within the transport industry, in the wood, paper and textile industry and agriculture, fishery and forestry. Reviews have called for long-term follow-up studies of population-based cohorts with spirometry assessments to evaluate lung function and incidence of COPD [4]. 

Considerable efforts have been made in Norway to prevent occupational lung disease, such as regulations regarding reduction and elimination of exposures, general protective measures, use of personal respiratory protection and medical surveillance. There is a need for estimates on the reduced disease burden and information on occupations still at risk of lung disease. This study aims to provide valid insights into the association between occupations and long-term lung function decline in a general population in Norway.

Snippet: Agusti et al. (21) studied patterns of gas exchange in response to exercise in asbestosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; they found more obstruction on exercise. These differences may relate to the underlying mor- phology of each process: asbestosis may include more airway disease and less pulmonary vascular involvement than other forms of pulmonary fibrosis. 

Asbestos exposure as a distinct cause of pulmonary obstruction is controversial because it is difficult to separate smoking as a confounder (19,22). In our patient, per- haps exposures to both asbestos and envi- ronmental tobacco smoke manifested in obstructive changes. Furthermore, it has been suggested that smoking and asbestos act synergistically to promote both restric- tive and obstructive pulmonary disease. For example, Neri et al. (22) studied shipyard workers who smoked and were exposed to asbestos: current smokers or ex-smokers with high profusion scores had more obstructive changes, as manifested by lower FEVI/FVC ratios, than current smokers or ex-smokers with low profusion scores and a shorter duration of smoking. Damage from smoking may decrease the ability to clear inhaled asbestos fibers and increase the per- meability of the airway walls, allowing easier penetration by asbestos fibers (23). 

HRCT scans are considered to be more sensitive than plain films for detecting inter- stitial fibrosis. There is growing evidence that through increased contrast resolution and axial image display, HRCT can detect both interstitial and pleural disease in advance of clinical symptoms or positive conventional clinical or radiographic studies (22,24). In addition, HRCT findings have a greater cor- relation with the duration of asbestos expo- sure (22), the presence of moderate to severe dyspnea, a high ILO chest X-ray classifica- tion, a low FVC, and a high concentration of macrophages and eosinophils in bron- choalveolar lavage fluid (25). In combined asbestos and cigarette smoke exposure, HRCT may play a role in distinguishing emphysematous lung destruction from peripheral interstitial changes of asbestosis (24).

A case-finding tool called the lung function questionnaire (LFQ) is being created to help doctors choose which patients should undergo spirometry testing to confirm the presence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Methods: Survey research study of 185 convenient sampling.
Results: The results were obtained using lung function questionnaire. Statistical analysis shows that there is prevalence of risk for COPD amongst the carpenters.
Conclusions: This study concludes that there is a risk of developing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in carpenters who are exposed to saw dust as more than half the samples have scored less than or equal to 18 which indicates the risk for COPD.

documents.title: Occupation and 11-year lung function decline in the HUNT Study
documents.snippet:
Occupational exposure to vapours, dust, gas and fumes (VGDF) can cause or exacerbate respiratory symptoms and lung disease [1,2]. It has been estimated that ~15% of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) cases are attributable to preventable occupational exposures [3]. 

Identifying high-risk occupations is important for implementing targeted interventions. Many studies have investigated exposure to VGDF, as summarized in reviews [4][5][6]. Further, a review outlined studies of VGDF identified by a jobexposure matrix [7]. Although occupational titles give a coarse exposure classification, as the harmful agent is not specified and exposure can vary within the same occupation, it provides important knowledge to target risk reduction measures. Few studies have examined lung function across a variety of jobs titles [8][9][10][11][12][13], an approach that increases the chance to detect all high-risk jobs. To our knowledge, only one study has provided longitudinal spirometry measurements [13], which enables the examination of intraindividual changes and enhances precision and validity. The study indicated a higher incidence of COPD within the transport industry, in the wood, paper and textile industry and agriculture, fishery and forestry. Reviews have called for long-term follow-up studies of population-based cohorts with spirometry assessments to evaluate lung function and incidence of COPD [4]. 

Considerable efforts have been made in Norway to prevent occupational lung disease, such as regulations regarding reduction and elimination of exposures, general protective measures, use of personal respiratory protection and medical surveillance. There is a need for estimates on the reduced disease burden and information on occupations still at risk of lung disease. This study aims to provide valid insights into the association between occupations and long-term lung function decline in a general population in Norway.

documents.title: A retired shipyard worker with rapidly progressive pulmonary interstitial fibrosis.
documents.snippet:
Agusti et al. (21) studied patterns of gas exchange in response to exercise in asbestosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; they found more obstruction on exercise. These differences may relate to the underlying mor- phology of each process: asbestosis may include more airway disease and less pulmonary vascular involvement than other forms of pulmonary fibrosis. 

Asbestos exposure as a distinct cause of pulmonary obstruction is controversial because it is difficult to separate smoking as a confounder (19,22). In our patient, per- haps exposures to both asbestos and envi- ronmental tobacco smoke manifested in obstructive changes. Furthermore, it has been suggested that smoking and asbestos act synergistically to promote both restric- tive and obstructive pulmonary disease. For example, Neri et al. (22) studied shipyard workers who smoked and were exposed to asbestos: current smokers or ex-smokers with high profusion scores had more obstructive changes, as manifested by lower FEVI/FVC ratios, than current smokers or ex-smokers with low profusion scores and a shorter duration of smoking. Damage from smoking may decrease the ability to clear inhaled asbestos fibers and increase the per- meability of the airway walls, allowing easier penetration by asbestos fibers (23). 

HRCT scans are considered to be more sensitive than plain films for detecting inter- stitial fibrosis. There is growing evidence that through increased contrast resolution and axial image display, HRCT can detect both interstitial and pleural disease in advance of clinical symptoms or positive conventional clinical or radiographic studies (22,24). In addition, HRCT findings have a greater cor- relation with the duration of asbestos expo- sure (22), the presence of moderate to severe dyspnea, a high ILO chest X-ray classifica- tion, a low FVC, and a high concentration of macrophages and eosinophils in bron- choalveolar lavage fluid (25). In combined asbestos and cigarette smoke exposure, HRCT may play a role in distinguishing emphysematous lung destruction from peripheral interstitial changes of asbestosis (24).

Title: Additive Synergism between Asbestos and Smoking in Lung Cancer Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Snippet: Asbestos exposure was arbitrarily taken as more than 100 air-borne fiber-yr/ml of environmental air for >5% of their work time and cigarette smoking was categorized as smokers who smoked >15 cigarettes/day. Those subjects having lower and shorter fiber exposures and lower cigarette consumption were deemed as non-exposed or non-smokers, respectively.

The meta-analysis of case-control and cohort studies were conducted separately due to differences in the nature of study design [42].

Title: Relative burden of lung and pleural cancers from exposure to asbestos: a cross-sectional analysis of occupational mortality in England and Wales
Snippet: We know from other research that smoking and asbestos interact in causing lung cancer, such that relative risks from the two causes in combination are more than additive. 8 9It follows that in a person with lung cancer who has been both a smoker and exposed to asbestos, the disease may be attributable to both causes (or put another way, avoidance of either of the exposures might have been sufficient to prevent the disease).However, with the method of statistical analysis that we employed, interactions between smoking and asbestos could be ignored.The parameter on which we focused was the difference between the number of deaths from lung cancer that actually occurred in the job group and the number that would have been expected if the job group had the smoking habits that it did, but no exposure to asbestos.That measure will have included excess deaths attributable to asbestos alone in non-smokers, and to the joint effects of smoking and asbestos as compared with smoking alone in smokers.

The variability that we found in the ratio of excess lung cancer to mesothelioma by job group may in part reflect differences by type of asbestos.Previous metaanalysis of cohort studies has suggested a lower ratio for crocidolite (0.7) than for chrysotile (6.1), amosite (4.0) and mixed fibres (1.9). 6However, intensity and timing of exposure could also be a factor, and might explain why, when we included mesotheliomas other than of the peritoneum, the mean ratio that we observed across all 22 job groups (0.28) was relatively low.Another analysis, based on national data for England and Wales during 1980-2000, suggested an intermediate ratio in the order of 0.67-1.0. 1 The disparity from our estimate may in part reflect differences in the methods used to control for confounding effects of smoking, but there may also have been changes over time in patterns of Open access exposure to asbestos, and a reduction in the prevalence of smoking in asbestos-exposed occupations (if the joint effect of asbestos and smoking on lung cancer is more than additive, then a given exposure to asbestos will cause more lung cancers in smokers than in the same number of non-smokers).

Title: Patterns of pulmonary dysfunction in asbestos workers: a cross-sectional study
Snippet: Two hundred seventy seven asbestos workers and 177 control subjects were included in the study ( Table 1). The participation rates for exposed and control subjects were not different: 77% and 80% respectively. The asbestos workers were significantly older than the controls. Smoking was more frequent among asbestos workers, and they also had smoked a greater number of pack years. Among the asbestos workers, 36% had radiographic changes consistent with emphysema, 31% with asbestosis, and 15% had CXR findings consistent with both asbestosis and emphysema.

As shown in figure 1, more than 80% of the controls had normal pulmonary function compared to only half of the asbestos workers had normal pulmonary function. Consequently, the proportions of subjects with obstructive, restrictive and mixed patterns of pulmonary dys- function in the exposed group were all higher than the corresponding proportions in the control group.

Although the PFT values except the FEV1/FVC ratio were adjusted for age and height, we also included age in the regression analysis as there was significant age difference between the exposed and control groups ( Table 2). Because we were interested in examining the effect of mere asbestos exposure (without CXR evidence of asbestosis) on patterns of pulmonary, we excluded patients with radiographic asbestosis from the model. After accounting for age and smoking, asbestos exposure was significantly associated with restrictive pattern of pulmonary dysfunction and decreased DLCO. However, asbestos exposure was not significantly associated with FEV1/ FVC ratio. Similar results were found when FEV1, FVC, and DLCO were regressed on exposure status and pack year without including age in the model (not shown).

As shown in Table 3, when PFT values were regressed on exposure status in non-smokers only, asbestos exposure was significantly associated with low FEV1, FVC and DLCO percent predicted values after accounting for age. In addition, the results indicate that non-smoking asbestos workers had close to 3% less FEV1/FVC ratios compared to non -smoker control workers of similar age and height. This last relationship, however, was not statistically significant. For FEV1, FVC and DLCO, the results were similar when age was excluded from the regression model as the PFT values were adjusted for age (analysis not shown).
